Washington Regulators Advance Medical Marijuana Verification Rulemaking Tied to Federal Registration, Rejecting Staff Recommendation

  • By Anthony Martinelli in News

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:18
Instaread

The Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board voted unanimously Wednesday to move forward with rulemaking that could allow licensed marijuana businesses to obtain state-issued certificates verifying their participation in Washington’s medical marijuana system, rejecting a recommendation from agency staff to deny the proposal.

The October 7 decision, signed by Board Chair Jim Vollendroff and members Ollie Garrett and Pete Holmes, approves a petition submitted by Caitlein Ryan and The Cannabis Alliance. The proposal seeks to establish a formal process for documenting businesses’ medical marijuana activities for purposes including federal registration, banking, research and insurance.

The vote marks a significant development for Washington’s marijuana industry as businesses navigate changing federal requirements, including a new Drug Enforcement Administration registration (DEA) pathway for qualifying state-authorized medical marijuana operations.

Washington operates an integrated licensing system in which medical and recreational marijuana businesses generally operate under the same licenses. Although retailers can obtain medical marijuana endorsements and producers and processors can participate in medical marijuana activities, the state currently lacks a standardized process for issuing official documentation confirming that participation.

The proposed Medical Cannabis Verification Certificate would address that gap by allowing licensees to request documentation of their regulatory status and authorized medical marijuana activities. Certificates would be based on state licensing and endorsement records, with coordination between the Liquor and Cannabis Board and Department of Health when necessary.

However, agency staff had recommended rejecting the petition, citing concerns about administrative costs, incomplete historical records and whether the certificates would satisfy federal requirements.

Staff warned that the board and Department of Health may lack sufficient information to independently verify a business’s past medical marijuana activities, potentially requiring reliance on self-reported information. They also argued that operating the program would require staffing and technical resources not currently included in the agency’s budget.

Perhaps most significantly, staff questioned whether certificates would help businesses obtain federal registration, given that Washington’s licensing system allows the same businesses to participate in both medical and recreational marijuana markets.

Despite those concerns, all three board members voted to accept the petition rather than follow the staff recommendation.

The decision does not immediately establish the certificate program or authorize businesses to obtain certificates. Instead, it begins the rulemaking process, during which the board can develop specific requirements and determine how verification would operate.
